title: Trump Hosts Xi at White House: AI, Trade Tensions & Taiwan Take Center Stage
body:
President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, marking a rare face‑to‑face encounter between the leaders of the United States and China amid a fragile trade truce and a growing contest for supremacy in artificial‑intelligence technology. The two‑day visit, which included a bilateral meeting, a working lunch and a state dinner, was intended to cement a tentative “tariff freeze” that has held since early 2024 and to open a dialogue on the strategic implications of AI, while also navigating the ever‑present flashpoint of Taiwan.

The opening ceremony took place on the South Lawn under a clear Washington sky, with the two presidents shaking hands while flanked by senior officials from both nations. Trump, who has repeatedly criticized mainstream media coverage of the event, posted a terse message on his Truth Social platform lamenting that networks such as CNN and MSNBC chose not to broadcast the arrival, calling the omission “made for television.” CBS, which did air the ceremony, reported that the optics of the meeting were carefully choreographed to convey a sense of diplomatic normalcy despite underlying tensions.

Trade policy dominated the early talks. Since the “Phase One” agreement of 2020, the two economies have been locked in a series of tit‑for‑tat tariffs that have strained global supply chains. In recent months, both sides have signaled a willingness to pause further escalations, with Trump’s administration proposing a six‑month extension of the current tariff moratorium in exchange for Chinese commitments on intellectual‑property protection and market access for American agricultural products. Xi’s delegation, led by Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, indicated a readiness to discuss “mutual benefit” but stopped short of offering concrete concessions on technology transfers, a point that remains a sticking‑point for Washington.

The AI rivalry was the second pillar of the agenda. In a joint statement, both leaders acknowledged that rapid advances in machine learning, generative models, and autonomous systems pose “significant opportunities and risks” for global stability. The United States, which has recently unveiled a new AI‑focused export‑control framework, urged China to adopt transparent standards and to refrain from weaponizing AI without international oversight. Beijing, for its part, emphasized the need for “fair competition” and warned against “unilateral restrictions” that could hamper its own innovation ecosystem. Observers note that while the dialogue was cordial, substantive agreements on AI governance remain elusive, reflecting deep mistrust over data security and the potential for algorithmic bias to be exploited in cyber‑espionage.

Taiwan, the perennial flashpoint, lingered in the background of every conversation. Trump reiterated his administration’s “One China” stance but also affirmed the United States’ commitment to the Taiwan Relations Act, which obligates Washington to provide defensive capabilities to the island. Xi, meanwhile, reiterated that any move toward formal independence would be “a red line” for Beijing. The two sides agreed to “maintain open channels” to prevent miscalculations, a diplomatic nicety that analysts say is more symbolic than substantive given the entrenched positions of both governments.

Political analysts see the visit as a calculated gamble by Trump to showcase his foreign‑policy credentials ahead of the 2028 election cycle, while also attempting to position the United States as a cooperative partner rather than an adversarial antagonist. Critics argue that the state dinner, replete with traditional American fare and a performance by a military band, was a veneer that masks the deeper strategic competition that will likely intensify as AI technologies mature and supply‑chain dependencies evolve.

Looking forward, the outcomes of this high‑profile meeting will be measured not by grand declarations but by the implementation of incremental steps: whether the tariff truce can be extended beyond the provisional timeline, how both capitals navigate the nascent AI regulatory landscape, and whether diplomatic channels can effectively manage Taiwan‑related crises. The world will be watching closely, as the trajectory set in Washington this week could shape the contours of U.S.–China relations for years to come.
